Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. In this section, we first provide an overview of the methods used for fruit localization and then we analyze how these methodologies are employed for yield estimation. 2.1. Object detection and counting for agriculture applications Fully supervised CNN architectures for detection and counting have achieved impressive results in a wide variety of datasets and tasks (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017; Khan et al., 2016; Bargoti and Un- derwood, 2017a). While their effectiveness is evident and extensively demonstrated, the need for massive amounts of data and supervision labels limits their practical applicability. For these reasons, weakly supervised methods have emerged as a viable and more convenient al- ternative: their objective is to guarantee performance comparable with fully-supervised baselines while relying on less informative

(2014) the authors extract hand- crafted features for fruit detection, i.e., Radial Symmetry Transform and Invariant Maximal Detector, from RGB stereo images collected by an Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV). These visual cues are used to localize the camera (and, as a consequence, the UGV) and detect fruits in grape orchards. Conversely, the strategy proposed in Roy and Isler (2016) uses a combination of Structure from Motion and SIFT/SURF features to predict apple sizes and perform counting. Since it is well known that hand-crafted features are not robust to image non-idealities, CNN models, which provide more robust descrip- tors, have become more popular even in agricultural contexts. In Stein et al. (2016) the authors present a yield estimation framework that combines the information from auxiliary sensors and the visual features extracted by a CNN. The proposed strategy is composed of a fruit detector based on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015), a LIDAR sensor and a GPS-RTK coupled with an inertial unit. Fruit matching, occlusions and multi-view errors are avoided by estimating the robot pose and by 3D positioning the detected fruits. Bargoti and Underwood (2017b) presents a solution that combines semantic segmentation maps, com- puted with a CNN architecture and a Multi Layer Perceptron, with GPS data. In the last years, researchers have focused on strategies that rely only on monocular cameras and remove the need for range and differ- ential positioning sensors. ## Análise da Pesquisa:

**1. Área Computacional:**

Redes Neurais Convolucionais / Deep Learning (O contexto menciona extensivo uso de CNNs para detecção de frutos e estimação de produção, incluindo arquiteturas como FasterRCNN).

**2. Sensores Utilizados:**

*   Câmera (RGB e estéreo)
*   LIDAR
*   GPS-RTK (combinado com unidade inercial)

**3. Bibliotecas, Frameworks ou Arquiteturas:**

*   FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015)
*   Multi Layer Perceptron
*   Structure from Motion
*   SIFT/SURF
*   Radial Symmetry Transform
*   Invariant Maximal Detector

**4. Solução / Tarefa Principal:**

Estimativa de produção (yield estimation) em aplicações agrícolas, com foco em detecção e localização de frutos.
